# Simulations {#sec-simulations}

This chapter summarises how the method performs in simulation, as of 14 November 2026. All numbers come from 1,000 replicates per scenario unless stated otherwise.

## How to read the results

- **Coverage** is the share of replicates whose 95% interval contains the true prevalence. With 1,000 replicates, Monte Carlo error alone puts a correct 95% procedure anywhere in **[93.6, 96.4]**. A coverage inside that band is not evidence of over- or under-coverage.
- **SE ratio** is the empirical SD of the estimates across replicates divided by the mean estimated SE. Near 1 means the standard errors are right; below 1 means they are too large.
- **$\hat K = 4$** is the share of replicates in which the merge step finds the true number of phenotypes. Unless stated otherwise, bias, SE ratio and coverage use only those replicates (with an unflagged SE).

## Populations

Both designs use four phenotypes in three biomarkers. The phenotype centroids sit at the corners of a square, $(\pm 2, \pm 2, \cdot)$, with diagonal covariances and standard deviations below 1. Phenotype membership depends on a person-level variable $x_2$ and on stratum and PSU random effects, so the design is informative and people in the same PSU resemble each other. Each design has four scenarios:

| Scenario | Change from base |
| :--- | :--- |
| base | Four well-separated Gaussian phenotypes |
| rare | Phenotype 4 at about 4.6% |
| skew | Biomarkers within each phenotype follow a standardised Gamma(2), same means and covariances |
| overlap | Centroids moved halfway towards the centre, so neighbouring phenotypes overlap |

## Design 1: the main design (4 PSUs per stratum)

Following Kim, Rao and Wang (2024, Supplement S9): 50 strata, about 1,250 PSUs of 150–225 people, $N \approx 200{,}000$. Stage 1 samples 4 PSUs per stratum with probability proportional to size; stage 2 samples people with probability proportional to $x_2$, for an overall sampling fraction of 1% ($n \approx 2{,}000$, 200 PSUs, df 150). PSU sizes vary little and do not affect the phenotypes, so the first stage is not informative.

These results were obtained before FOLD was adopted, with an earlier merge rule (`simulations/night/report_prod.txt`); FOLD has not yet been run on this design. They show how the sandwich behaves when the phenotypes are recovered:

| Scenario | $\hat K = 4$ | SE ratio | Coverage by phenotype | Mean coverage |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| base | 99.8% | 0.99–1.03 | 95.0 / 93.1 / 94.6 / 94.2 | 94.2 |
| rare | 99.5% | 0.92–1.01 | 95.3 / 92.4 / 94.5 / 96.2 | 94.6 |
| skew | 71.2% | 0.80–0.85 | 83.9 / 87.0 / 92.9 / 81.1 | 86.2 |
| overlap (52 replicates only) | 51.9% | 0.97–2.38 | 87.0 / 76.1 / 69.6 / 84.8 | 79.3 |

## Design 2: informative PSU sizes, 2 PSUs per stratum

Folder `simulations/psusize_design/`. This design is closer to NHANES, which samples 2 PSUs per stratum. It follows the population of Zhou, Elliott and Raghunathan (2016) as used in the survey-martingale project:

- 50 strata with a stratum effect $\gamma_h \sim \text{Unif}(-0.87, 0.87)$; PSU sizes from 69 to 1,529 (coefficient of variation 0.63), larger in strata with larger $\gamma_h$; $N = 482{,}392$ in 1,528 PSUs.
- Phenotype 1 becomes more common as PSU size grows (23%, 33%, 41% across size tertiles), so the first stage is informative.
- Stage 1 samples 2 PSUs per stratum with probability proportional to size (Brewer's method); stage 2 samples 1% of the stratum by systematic PPS on $x_2$, with exact inclusion probabilities. $n \approx 4{,}828$, 100 PSUs, df 50.

### Results with FOLD

`fold_unweighted` with the height-gap cut:

| Scenario | $\hat K = 4$ | Replicates used | Largest bias | SE ratio | Coverage by phenotype | Mean coverage |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| base | 100% | 1,000 | 0.0009 | 0.97–1.02 | 94.2 / 93.7 / 94.7 / 96.1 | 94.7 |
| rare | 100% | 1,000 | 0.0008 | 0.99–1.01 | 94.4 / 94.4 / 94.0 / 96.3 | 94.8 |
| skew | 97.9% | 971 | 0.024 | 0.78–0.89 | 77.2 / 87.1 / 91.1 / 67.0 | 80.6 |
| overlap | **30.8%** | 305 | 0.005 | 0.78–1.03 | 95.1 / 92.1 / 95.7 / 93.1 | 94.0 |

## What the results show

**Base and rare: calibrated.** When the phenotypes are distinct, FOLD recovers them in every replicate, bias is under 0.001, SE ratios are within a few percent of 1, and coverage is at the nominal level. The design with 2 PSUs per stratum did not cost coverage.

**Skew: a bias that does not shrink.** People in the tail of a skewed phenotype are assigned to its neighbour. This biases the prevalences by up to about 0.02, and the bias does not fall with sample size while the standard errors do, so coverage drops to about 81–86%. It comes from fitting skewed groups with Gaussians, not from the merge: FOLD finds four groups in 98% of replicates, and the earlier merge rule on Design 1 shows the same bias. The standard errors are too large, not too small (SE ratio about 0.8).

**Overlap: the cut is the issue.** Among replicates that find four groups, coverage is at the nominal level. The problem is how often four groups are found. With FOLD, the tree of merges almost always contains the right four groups, but the height-gap cut often stops at two or three.

## Choosing the FOLD cut

The FOLD tree of 60 skew and 60 overlap samples (20 for base and rare) was cut with several rules. Samples with four groups, unweighted tree:

| Cut | base (20) | rare (20) | skew (60) | overlap (60) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $\gamma_{\text{AVG}}$ | 20 | 19 | 59 | 45 |
| Height gap | 20 | 20 | 60 | 16 |
| Elbow (largest drop in $r$) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Largest relative drop in $r$ | 20 | 18 | 41 | 20 |

- The tree itself is right: its four-group level has one phenotype per group in 60 of 60 skew samples and 58 of 60 overlap samples.
- $\gamma_{\text{AVG}}$, the default of @dombowsky2025fold, is the most even across scenarios and has no tuning constant.

**Coarser answers are still correct answers.** When a cut stops early on overlap, the groups it reports are almost always unions of whole phenotypes (59 of 60 at two and at three groups). A three-group answer that merges two overlapping phenotypes estimates their combined prevalence. Scoring replicates at the level they report, against the true phenotypes merged the same way, is in progress (@sec-phenotypes).

## Pending runs

Submitted 14 November 2026, results expected around 16–17 November:

- FOLD with the $\gamma_{\text{AVG}}$ cut on all four scenarios of Design 2, saving results at every $\hat K$.
- FOLD with the height-gap cut on overlap, rerun to save results at every $\hat K$.

These will give bias and coverage for $\gamma_{\text{AVG}}$, and coverage at the coarser levels.
